sources.citation: McElhanon, Kenneth A. 1970. The Selepet language within the Finisterre-Huon phylum (New Guinea). PhD thesis, Australian National University (466-page scan; ANU Open Research 1885/109875).
sources.quote: Chapter 3 is the B-14 text verbatim ('A stress group contains one primary stress occurring on the initial syllable followed by secondary stresses occurring on subsequent alternate syllables...'). §4.9 adds that under the MID-HIGH (inquiry) contour 'the stress group manifesting the nucleus may exhibit regressive perturbation of the primary stress ... rather than the primary stress occurring on the initial syllable of the stress group, it may occur on subsequent syllables which usually manifest secondary stresses' (intonational, not lexical).
sources.locator: ch.3 'Selepet Phonology' §5 Stress group, chapter pp.13-14 (PDF p.123f); §4.9 Inquiry (same page) on intonational perturbation
sources.note: Glottolog's top-ranked 'grammar' (487 pp) for Selepet; its phonology chapter is the B-14 text verbatim, so it adds nothing to the coding but closes the 'is there a bigger grammar' question. fetched sources now.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K.A. 1967. Selepet vocoid clusters. In Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 6, Pacific Linguistics A-12, pp.1-18. Canberra: ANU. (ANU Open Research 1885/254254)
sources.quote: 'Non-phonemic stress accompanied by high pitch occurs in a predictable manner with primary stress occurring on the first syllable and secondary stress occurring on the following alternate syllables. In three and five syllable words the final secondary stress is optional. Grammatical perturbation of stress has been observed but does not yield any stress patterns which would provide additional information.' Then (a) two-syllable: primary on first (seduk, pato, awun); (b) three-syllable: primary on first, secondary optionally on third (galagat); (c) four-syllable: primary on first, secondary on t
sources.note: Earlier statement by the same author that pins the optionality to the word-final secondary in odd-parity words ('In three and five syllable words the final secondary stress is optional') and states stress is non-phonemic with high pitch; useful as a second citation for the optional-secondary note in 'corr'. fetched sources now.
